title: Russian-owned NIS refinery halted by US sanctions, exposing Serbia's fuel supply
programme: Sale of majority stake in NIS to Gazprom (2009)
problem: Serbia's only oil refinery, NIS, has been majority Russian-owned since Gazprom bought 51% of its shares in 2009, which exposed it to sanctions on Russian firms.
solution: Serbia sold control of NIS to Gazprom and kept a minority stake; Russian shareholders now hold 56.15% and the Serbian state 29.87%.
results: When US sanctions took effect on 9 October 2025, Croatia's JANAF stopped buying from NIS and production halted completely. NIS supplies up to 80% of motor fuels consumed in Serbia, employs 14,000 people and contributed roughly €2 billion to Serbia's 2024 budget.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own case: foreign state ownership of critical energy infrastructure turned into a supply and fiscal risk. The source suggests a forced sale and equity participation by EU firms.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need a legal route to buy out the Russian stake, most likely its Expropriation Law, and a buyer for the shares.
blockers: Gazprom has not agreed to sell, and so far only Hungary's MOL Group has shown interest in investing.
quote: The Serbian oil refinery stopped production completely following US sanctions that targeted all Russian-owned oil refineries, leaving the Serbian transport sector at risk.

title: Serbia cut Russian gas share to 82% but progress stalled
problem: All the gas consumed in Serbia came from Russia before the invasion of Ukraine, and Serbia is also the transit route for Bosnia and Herzegovina's gas.
solution: Serbia established links with Azerbaijan's gas suppliers to replace part of its Russian gas.
results: Serbia's dependence on Russian gas fell from 100% in 2021 to 82% in 2024. In 2025, before the US sanctions took effect, Serbia held talks on extending its Russian gas contract for another three to ten years.
serbia_reason: Serbia's own diversification has moved slowly while North Macedonia switched fully to Azerbaijani gas by 2025. The EU plans to phase out Russian gas completely by 2028.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need long-term contracts with non-Russian suppliers and access to global LNG through neighbouring infrastructure.
blockers: The source says political will in Serbia has been lacking, and Azerbaijan's limited production may not remove Russian leverage.
quote: In Serbia, which is a gas corridor for gas supplies to Bosnia and Herzegovina, little progress has been made. For this change to happen, political will in Serbia is essential, but has been lacking.

title: Western Balkan market coupling by 2027 is unrealistic despite Serbia's lead
programme: EU Growth Plan for the Western Balkans – electricity market coupling
problem: Coupling with EU electricity markets requires transposing the Energy Community Electricity Integration Package, adopting an NECP, running a day-ahead market and certifying an independent TSO, a heavy task for small administrations.
solution: The 2024–2028 EU Growth Plan for the Western Balkans set 2027 as the goal for coupling, subject to alignment with EU law. Serbia is the frontrunner, having adopted a comprehensive set of primary and secondary acts for full transposition.
funding: Coupling is facilitated by the EU Growth Plan for the Western Balkans, whose €6 billion the source calls modest for the region's needs.
results: Serbia scored 58% on regulatory readiness for coupling, behind North Macedonia at 61%. All Western Balkan countries missed the 31 December 2023 transposition deadline, and an 18-month technical preparation must follow verification.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own accession-linked reform, and coupling plus an equivalent carbon price is the route to avoid CBAM on electricity exports. The source calls for more IPA funding for capacity in ministries and regulators.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need more staff and technical capacity in its ministry and regulator to finish verification and the technical preparation for coupling.
blockers: Limited administrative capacity, complex regulations and the separate CBAM requirement for a carbon price equivalent to the EU's slow progress.
quote: Considering the current state of transposition and the timeline after transposition, it is safe to conclude that electricity coupling between the EU and the Western Balkans by 2027, as foreseen in the countries’ growth plans, is not realistic.

title: Montenegro's €24/tCO2 ETS price falls far short of CBAM equivalence
problem: CBAM charges electricity imported from the Western Balkans at default emission factors, an expected €70–€80 per MWh, unless a country has a power-sector carbon price equivalent to the EU ETS by 2030.
solution: Montenegro introduced an emissions trading system, the only one in the Western Balkans, which could support a CBAM exemption under Article 2(7) if its price reaches EU levels.
results: Montenegro's carbon price is €24/tCO2, against an EU price of around €80/tCO2, which the source says shows how hard it is to close the gap.
serbia_reason: Serbia must meet the same CBAM exemption condition of an EU-equivalent carbon price for power by 2030. Montenegro shows that having an ETS is not enough if the price stays low.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need a carbon price path that reaches EU levels by 2030, not just a new instrument.
blockers: A price near €80/tCO2 would sharply raise costs for lignite-based generation.
quote: Only Montenegro, the smallest Western Balkan economy, currently has an ETS, but with a carbon price of €24/tCO2, illustrating the difficulties in adjusting the price to the levels applicable in the EU, currently around €80/tCO2.

title: Serbia lacks a binding coal phase-out timeline, protecting cheap SOE lignite
problem: Serbia depends heavily on lignite, yet the 2020 Sofia Declaration commits the region to climate neutrality by 2050, which cannot be reached without phasing lignite out of power.
solution: Serbia's adopted NECP aims to gradually reduce lignite, expand wind and solar and add gas capacity and efficiency measures, but sets no phase-out date.
results: Outside North Macedonia and Montenegro, coal's share of power in the region fell only a few percentage points between 2014 and 2024, and coal-based electricity per capita shows no downward trend. Serbia, like Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, lacks a binding timeline.
serbia_reason: Cheap, often subsidised lignite power from state-owned enterprises keeps household prices low, which makes a phase-out politically costly. Without a date, Serbia's power exports face high CBAM costs.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to set and commit to a phase-out timeline, using the revised Green Agenda Action Plan 2025–2030 as a toolkit.
blockers: Low household electricity prices rest on cheap state-owned lignite generation, so a phase-out carries political costs.
quote: The National Energy Climate Plans (NECPs) of Western Balkan countries confirm that the coal phase-out is not planned any time soon. Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Kosovo continue to depend heavily on coal and lack binding timelines.

title: North Macedonia commits to coal exit, converting Oslomej to solar
programme: North Macedonia NECP coal phase-out (Oslomej solar conversion, Bitola decommissioning)
problem: North Macedonia's power system relied on lignite plants, and most Western Balkan countries had no national coal phase-out date.
solution: Its adopted NECP commits to close all coal plants by 2030, converting the Oslomej coal plant into a solar plant and decommissioning Bitola, with solar, wind, hydro and gas backup replacing them.
results: Coal's share of North Macedonia's electricity mix fell by 26.8 percentage points from 2014 to 2024. This largely meant greater dependence on gas, which now accounts for almost a quarter of the mix.
serbia_reason: This neighbour, with a similar lignite legacy, is the only one with an operational coal exit commitment in its NECP. It also shows the risk of swapping lignite for gas.
adapt_needed: Serbia's much larger lignite fleet would need a staged, plant-by-plant version, with site conversion to solar where grid connections already exist.
blockers: Serbia's lignite fleet is far larger and underpins low tariffs, so replacement capacity and the political cost are much greater.
quote: Only North Macedonia has an operational coal phase-out commitment, aiming to convert one coal-fired plant (TE Plant Oslomej) into a solar plant and to decommission the other (Bitola).

title: Montenegro's €87.5m Pljevlja upgrade pushes coal exit from 2035 to 2040–2041
problem: Montenegro's single coal plant, TE Pljevlja, together with wood burning for heating and motor vehicles, has been causing severe health issues.
solution: Montenegro decided to invest €87.5 million in upgrading the plant instead of closing it by its earlier 2035 pledge.
results: The renovation may cut the plant's carbon footprint and especially local air pollutants, but planned closure moved from 2035 to 2040–2041, which the source says conflicts with the coal phase-out goal.
serbia_reason: Serbia faces the same choice between costly pollution retrofits on lignite units and earlier closure. Montenegro shows that a retrofit can lock in years of extra coal operation.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to weigh retrofit costs against closure dates and CBAM exposure before committing capital.
blockers: Retrofits are attractive because they cut local pollution and keep cheap domestic power running.
quote: Montenegro plans the closure of its coal plant by 2040–2041, though it previously pledged 2035. The delay owes to the decision to invest €87.5 million in upgrading its single coal-plant (TE Pljevlja), which, together with wood burning for domestic heating and motor vehicles, has been causing severe health issues (Doderovic et al, 2021).
